To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) HPV integration is a frequent event in high-grade cervical lesions; (ii) the detection of integrated HPV DNA may have a role in clinical testing of HPV-associated cervical neoplasms; (iii) the use of tyramide reagent for in situ hybridization is a sensitive and reliable method for detection of HPV integration.
HPV integration is a common event in cervical neoplasias, and that the presence of integrated HPV is associated with a higher likelihood of progression to invasive carcinoma.

(a) HPV is a necessary cause of invasive cervical carcinoma; (b) the presence of HPV in cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is not a reliable predictor of progression, and that HPV integration is a potential marker of disease progression; (c) HPV integration may be detected by in situ hybridisation, and this method is suitable for use on clinical specimens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of HPV integration in cervical neoplasms and the potential clinical application of in situ hybridization for detection of HPV integration.
the detection of high-risk HPV and the physical status of its DNA in intraepithelially neoplastic cells, using a novel in situ hybridization technique.
the development of a sensitive and specific method for detection of HPV integration in cervical lesions and its potential application to the clinical setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV testing in cervical cancer is an important adjunct to cytology, and should be used in the triage of women with equivocal cytology.
HPV integration is not an indicator of progression to invasive cancer, but rather an indicator of the presence of an HPV-associated lesion.
HPV testing in the clinical setting is not yet ready for prime time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a highly sensitive in situ hybridisation method that allows detection of integrated HPV in formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissue sections, and that we are currently using this to investigate the prevalence of HPV integration in cervical neoplasias.
we have shown that HPV DNA is integrated in 50-70% of high-grade cervical lesions.
HPV is a necessary cause of neoplasia but is not sufficient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tyramide signal amplification (TSA) in situ hybridization can be used to detect integrated HPV and that this technique may be of value in clinical testing for HPV-associated neoplastic disease.
tyramide-based in situ hybridization is a highly sensitive and specific technique for the detection of HPV integration in cervical neoplasms.
the use of in situ hybridization to detect HPV DNA in situ can provide important data relevant to clinical testing for high-risk HPV.
